title: Modal particles
schema: english-prompt -> learner types German -> Reveal/Hide answer shows reference + speaker

exercises.english: Would you please come along with us?
exercises.german: Komm doch bitte mit uns!
exercises.why: Imperative plus unstressed doch right after the imperative verb: an urgent nudge, not a question.

exercises.english: You did tell me that.
exercises.german: Das hast du doch gesagt.
exercises.why: Perfect with the conjugated auxiliary in position II, and doch in the Mittelfeld after the object.

exercises.english: I have told you that already, haven't I?
exercises.german: Ich habe es dir doch schon gesagt.
exercises.why: The particle cannot end the sentence, so it moves into the Mittelfeld between the objects and schon.

exercises.english: The train does leave at eight, doesn't it?
exercises.german: Der Zug fährt doch um acht ab.
exercises.why: Ablösende abfahren splits into ab + fährt in the sentence; doch softens the contradiction to a listener.

exercises.english: That is exactly what I said.
exercises.german: Genau das habe ich doch gesagt.
exercises.why: Heavy topic als Genau das first; the particle follows the auxiliary in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: You did forget your keys again, didn't you?
exercises.german: Du hast deine Schlüssel doch wieder vergessen!
exercises.why: An accusative object in the Mittelfeld pushes doch in front of the participle wieder vergessen.

exercises.english: Do wait a moment, will you?
exercises.german: Warte doch einen Moment!
exercises.why: Modal particles can follow the imperative form, which is why doch stands here behind warte.

exercises.english: It won't take long, will it?
exercises.german: Das wird doch nicht lange dauern.
exercises.why: Future auxiliaries also attract particles, and doch directly before the negation negates the estimate.

exercises.english: Let's just take a taxi, shall we?
exercises.german: Lass uns doch einfach ein Taxi nehmen.
exercises.why: In the lassen construction the infinitive goes to the end, so doch sits inside the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: You only had to ask me.
exercises.german: Du hättest mich doch nur fragen müssen.
exercises.why: Konjunktiv II plus modal infinitive; doch before nur strengthens the reproach about what was missing.

exercises.english: I would not have thought that!
exercises.german: Das hätte ich doch nicht gedacht!
exercises.why: Aubitive hätte plus negation; the particle marks the surprising expectation being contradicted.

exercises.english: I am telling you that it will turn out that way.
exercises.german: Ich sage dir doch, dass es so kommen wird.
exercises.why: A particle can introduce a dass-clause, but here it stays in the main clause before dass.

exercises.english: Do be a little less stubborn about it.
exercises.german: Sei doch bitte nicht so stur.
exercises.why: Imperative with particle plus politeness adverb; doch reduces the sharpness of the command.

exercises.english: She is coming after all, isn't she?
exercises.german: Sie kommt doch tatsächlich.
exercises.why: tatsächlich and doch combine: the speaker withdraws an earlier assumption instead of insisting.

exercises.english: But I told you the opposite!
exercises.german: Aber ich habe dir doch das Gegenteil gesagt!
exercises.why: Explicit contradiction; the unstressed doch is never written in capitals to show emphasis.

exercises.english: You can see that I am right, can't you?
exercises.german: Siehst du doch, dass ich recht habe.
exercises.why: After the finite verb the particle may stand directly before the dass-clause, with no comma.

exercises.english: You could have told me earlier, couldn't you?
exercises.german: Du hättest mir doch früher Bescheid sagen können.
exercises.why: Modal infinitive at the end keeps the particle far from the end, in the middle of the clause.

exercises.english: Would you mind opening the window?
exercises.german: Mach doch bitte das Fenster auf.
exercises.why: Separable verb aufmachen: the particle attaches after the imperative, not after the prefix.

exercises.english: It won't turn out that badly, will it?
exercises.german: So schlimm wird es doch nicht werden.
exercises.why: Comparative degree in the subject, with doch placed directly in front of the negation.

exercises.english: If you do hurry, we'll miss the train.
exercises.german: Wenn du dich doch beeilst, verpassen wir den Zug.
exercises.why: Position I particle after the wenn-clause: the comma is obligatory, and the focus falls on verpassen.

exercises.english: Come here for a moment!
exercises.german: Komm mal her!
exercises.why: Komm her would be a command; mal makes the same sentence a casual, friendly request.

exercises.english: Let's have a look at what that is.
exercises.german: Schauen wir mal, was das ist.
exercises.why: Wir-subject sentence: the particle follows the finite verb, marking a brief, informal procedure.

exercises.english: Take a break for a moment.
exercises.german: Mach mal eine Pause.
exercises.why: One-off suggestion; mal is the softened counterpart of the plain imperative.

exercises.english: I heard from you again, by the way.
exercises.german: Ich habe mal wieder etwas von dir gehört.
exercises.why: An idiomatic connector meaning by the way, sitting between the two verb elements.

exercises.english: Could you call me later?
exercises.german: Rufst du mich mal später an?
exercises.why: Separable verb anrufen: the particle cannot split verb and prefix and must follow the finite part.

exercises.english: How was it again with the appointment?
exercises.german: Wie war das noch mal mit dem Termin?
exercises.why: A fixed search expression, noch mal paired with a question word in position I.

exercises.english: Tell me, did you see the key?
exercises.german: Sag mal, hast du den Schlüssel gesehen?
exercises.why: The particle doubles as a discourse opener, like a comma-marked parenthetical after the imperative.

exercises.english: We need to talk about your plans at some point.
exercises.german: Wir müssen mal über deine Pläne reden.
exercises.why: Modal verb müssen with the particle in front of it: müssen mal, not mal müssen.

exercises.english: That was quite a surprise!
exercises.german: Das war ja eine Überraschung!
exercises.why: ja states that the surprise is shared knowledge, a frequent reaction particle.

exercises.english: You did say you were coming.
exercises.german: Du hast ja gesagt, dass du kommst.
exercises.why: ja points to something the hearer should recall, and a dass-clause follows the particle.

exercises.english: We have talked about that before.
exercises.german: Wir haben ja schon darüber gesprochen.
exercises.why: Akkusativ with a preposition plus ja, which keeps the anaphoric link to the shared past.

exercises.english: Don't help me with your excuses!
exercises.german: Hilf mir ja nicht mit deinen Ausreden!
exercises.why: Here ja is emphatic, not additive: negated, it intensifies the rejection.

exercises.english: Don't do anything silly!
exercises.german: Mach ja keinen Unsinn!
exercises.why: ja in front of a negation can signal a warning rather than a factual concession.

exercises.english: Just be careful, I don't have time.
exercises.german: Pass nur auf, ich habe ja keine Zeit.
exercises.why: The second clause needs no particle itself; ja highlights the scarce resource.

exercises.english: Tell me, did you really mean that?
exercises.german: Sag mal, hast du das wirklich ernst gemeint?
exercises.why: Two sentence features combined: an informal opener and a perfekt clause in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: Will you call me later, then?
exercises.german: Rufst du mich dann mal später an?
exercises.why: The particle sits in the Mittelfeld between the two pronouns and the temporal adverb.

exercises.english: Let's talk about Tuesday for a moment.
exercises.german: Lass uns mal über den Dienstag sprechen.
exercises.why: Particle after the accusative pronoun in the lassen construction.

exercises.english: He really is completely right.
exercises.german: Der hat ja wirklich völlig recht.
exercises.why: Perfect tense, where ja asserts the obvious rightness of the judgement just made.

exercises.english: Try that out, it tastes better.
exercises.german: Probier das mal aus, das schmeckt besser.
exercises.why: Bare imperative in the first clause, main-clause statement in the second, particle in between.

exercises.english: We haven't seen each other for a long time!
exercises.german: Wir haben uns ja lange nicht gesehen!
exercises.why: Reflexive reciprocal pronoun in the Akkusativ; ja draws attention to the shared fact.

exercises.english: Then just eat less.
exercises.german: Dann iss halt weniger.
exercises.why: halt changes an open demand into resigned acceptance of a fact.

exercises.english: It is just the way it is.
exercises.german: Es ist halt, wie es ist.
exercises.why: Parallel-clause comparison with a comma before wie, and halt carrying resignation.

exercises.english: We just have to get on with it.
exercises.german: Wir müssen halt mit dem Leben klarkommen.
exercises.why: Particle in front of the modal verb müssen, with a separable verb later in the clause.

exercises.english: Such a shame, nothing helps at all.
exercises.german: So ein Mist, da hilft halt nichts mehr.
exercises.why: An exclamation followed by a da-clause; halt softens the helplessness.

exercises.english: That was just a stupid idea.
exercises.german: Das war eben eine dumme Idee.
exercises.why: eben stresses that the judgement concerns exactly this single case.

exercises.english: We have only just talked.
exercises.german: Wir haben uns eben erst unterhalten.
exercises.why: eben in its temporal reading, just now, before erst: it signals the latest action.

exercises.english: Precisely for that reason we should start earlier.
exercises.german: Eben darum sollten wir früher anfangen.
exercises.why: eben as an emphatic point particle before a prepositional phrase, not as just.

exercises.english: He just wasn't lucky.
exercises.german: Er hat eben kein Glück gehabt.
exercises.why: Perfect tense, with eben dismissing the outcome as a one-off piece of bad luck.

exercises.english: All right, you're right after all.
exercises.german: Na gut, du hast halt recht.
exercises.why: halt concedes a point the speaker has just lost after a disagreement.

exercises.english: You just have to take risks sometimes.
exercises.german: Man muss halt ab und zu Risiken eingehen.
exercises.why: Generic man-clause: halt generalises the admission beyond the single case.

exercises.english: That was simply too much for us.
exercises.german: Das war eben zu viel für uns.
exercises.why: eben limits the statement to what just happened, not to the general situation.

exercises.english: He only just returned the book.
exercises.german: Er hat das Buch eben erst zurückgegeben.
exercises.why: Temporal eben, with the two time adverbs eben erst marking a very recent action.

exercises.english: You simply can't control every situation.
exercises.german: Du kannst halt nicht jede Situation kontrollieren.
exercises.why: Negated modal sentence where halt acknowledges a permanent limitation.

exercises.english: Exactly for that reason we're going earlier.
exercises.german: Eben deshalb gehen wir früher.
exercises.why: The particle highlights the immediate link to the reason just given.

exercises.english: We'll just wait until everyone is there.
exercises.german: Wir warten halt, bis alle da sind.
exercises.why: A bis-clause in position I, with the particle marking passive waiting in the main clause.

exercises.english: The bus just didn't run today, that's all.
exercises.german: Der Bus ist halt heute einmal ausgefallen.
exercises.why: Auffallen, a separable verb, with the particle before the temporal phrase.

exercises.english: It's just not that easy.
exercises.german: Das ist eben nicht so einfach.
exercises.why: Negation plus eben downgrades the expectation of an easy solution.

exercises.english: We're in the same seminar after all.
exercises.german: Wir sitzen eben im selben Seminar.
exercises.why: eben frames the shared seminar as the obvious reason for the situation being discussed.

exercises.english: That's exactly what I mean.
exercises.german: Eben das meine ich.
exercises.why: Particle in the focus position at the very front of the declarative sentence.

exercises.english: If it just doesn't work, then so be it.
exercises.german: Wenn es halt nicht geht, dann eben nicht.
exercises.why: Double use: halt concedes the failure, the second eben accepts it without protest.

exercises.english: You must have missed the first lesson.
exercises.german: Du hast wohl die erste Stunde verpasst.
exercises.why: wohl as an epistemic particle turns a complaint into a guess about the cause.

exercises.english: It's probably raining again.
exercises.german: Es regnet wohl schon wieder.
exercises.why: Wohl softens the bad news here; the particle comes before the temporal adverb schon.

exercises.english: She probably won't come anymore.
exercises.german: Sie kommt wohl nicht mehr.
exercises.why: A pre-negated verb, which pushes the particle to the very start of the clause.

exercises.english: That's probably not so important.
exercises.german: Das ist wohl nicht so wichtig.
exercises.why: Negation follows the particle; wohl lowers the speaker's estimate of the issue.

exercises.english: Actually, I wanted to call you today.
exercises.german: Eigentlich wollte ich dich heute anrufen.
exercises.why: eigentlich as a correction of the hearer's assumption about what the speaker meant.

exercises.english: We're actually meeting at eight.
exercises.german: Wir treffen uns eigentlich um acht.
exercises.why: Delayed qualification of the time: eigentlich softens the correction.

exercises.english: Actually, you should sleep more.
exercises.german: Eigentlich solltest du mehr schlafen.
exercises.why: Modal verb with the particle in front of it, undercutting a stated intention.

exercises.english: Where actually is my book?
exercises.german: Wo ist denn eigentlich mein Buch?
exercises.why: Two particles in a wh-question: denn addresses the listener, eigentlich the search itself.

exercises.english: He probably forgot half of it.
exercises.german: Er hat wohl die Hälfte vergessen.
exercises.why: Akkusativ object, with the epistemic particle between auxiliary and participle.

exercises.english: The restaurant was probably fully booked.
exercises.german: Das Restaurant war wohl ausgebucht.
exercises.why: Sein with a predicate adjective: the particle carries the inference about the reason.

exercises.english: Actually, one correction is still missing.
exercises.german: Eigentlich fehlt noch eine Korrektur.
exercises.why: Reversal of a presumption, a typical function of the discourse particle eigentlich.

exercises.english: When does the lecture actually begin?
exercises.german: Wann beginnt eigentlich die Vorlesung?
exercises.why: The verb comes directly after the question word, and eigentlich follows it in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: I probably mixed up two appointments.
exercises.german: Ich habe wohl zwei Termine verwechselt.
exercises.why: Akkusativ plural object, with wohl placed after the auxiliary habe.

exercises.english: Actually, I'd rather have Friday.
exercises.german: Eigentlich möchte ich lieber am Freitag.
exercises.why: Konjunktiv-like möchte plus a second degree: eigentlich opens a preference revision.

exercises.english: The colleague must have fallen ill.
exercises.german: Der Kollege ist wohl krank geworden.
exercises.why: A conclusion from visible evidence, the classic use of wohl with a sein perfect.

exercises.english: Actually, we still need two seats.
exercises.german: Eigentlich brauchen wir noch zwei Plätze.
exercises.why: brauchen takes an Akkusativ object; the particle introduces a factual reservation.

exercises.english: She probably didn't notice any of it.
exercises.german: Sie hat wohl nichts davon gemerkt.
exercises.why: Pronoun nichts, which takes the front slot and carries the negation here.

exercises.english: Actually, I haven't seen him for a long time.
exercises.german: Eigentlich habe ich ihn lange nicht gesehen.
exercises.why: Perfect with the full verb, where eigentlich reveals the speaker's neglected intention.

exercises.english: That was probably a spontaneous decision.
exercises.german: Das war wohl eine spontane Entscheidung.
exercises.why: An inference about a past situation, with wohl in front of the Akkusativ subject complement.

exercises.english: Actually, we should report that earlier.
exercises.german: Eigentlich sollten wir das früher melden.
exercises.why: Modal infinitive at the end, with the particle marking the forgotten duty.

exercises.english: I told you yesterday that it would be difficult.
exercises.german: Ich habe dir doch gestern gesagt, dass es schwierig wird.
exercises.why: Perfect with the full verb in position II; the particle slides into the Mittelfeld after gestern.

exercises.english: I would probably have come earlier.
exercises.german: Ich wäre wohl früher gekommen.
exercises.why: Konjunktiv II of sein, with the particle in front of the temporal adverb.

exercises.english: Could you close the window for a moment?
exercises.german: Könntest du mal bitte das Fenster schließen?
exercises.why: Modal verb in position II, and the particle must precede the modal, not follow it.

exercises.english: If you actually wanted to, you would have said so.
exercises.german: Wenn du es eigentlich gewollt hättest, hättest du es gesagt.
exercises.why: A comma is obligatory before a particle in position I of the main clause after a subordinate clause.

exercises.english: You are coming with me, aren't you?
exercises.german: Du kommst doch mit, oder?
exercises.why: A disjunction tag closes the sentence, so the particle can never be the last element itself.

exercises.english: You would probably not have noticed the difference.
exercises.german: Du hättest den Unterschied wohl nicht bemerkt.
exercises.why: The negation follows the particle, and a Modalpartikel may never be the final word.

exercises.english: You can simply ask me, can't you?
exercises.german: Du kannst mich doch einfach fragen.
exercises.why: Modal verb with the particle before it, and a separable verb later in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: We should actually talk about that once.
exercises.german: Wir sollten eigentlich mal darüber sprechen.
exercises.why: Two particles in the Mittelfeld, placed before the modal verb and before the separable verb.

exercises.english: She is probably right.
exercises.german: Sie hat wohl recht.
exercises.why: Short sentence: the particle can occupy the slot directly after the auxiliary.

exercises.english: You can count on me, of course.
exercises.german: Du kannst dich ja auf mich verlassen.
exercises.why: After a reflexive verb, ja reads as a reassurance and stays in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: You should have come earlier, then.
exercises.german: Dann hättest du eben früher kommen sollen.
exercises.why: A modal infinitive at the end means the particle has to move far to the left, right after hättest.

exercises.english: Could you introduce me to her?
exercises.german: Könntest du mich ihr wohl mal vorstellen?
exercises.why: Akkusativ and Dativ pronouns precede the two particles in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: Have you been there before?
exercises.german: Bist du da doch schon mal gewesen?
exercises.why: Perfect tense; the particles stay inside the Mittelfeld and the participle closes the sentence.

exercises.english: I have heard that before, haven't I?
exercises.german: Das habe ich doch schon gehört.
exercises.why: Akkusativ subject first, auxiliary in position II, particle in the Mittelfeld, participle last.

exercises.english: Then why are you still sitting here?
exercises.german: Dann sitzt du ja immer noch hier.
exercises.why: Adverb at the end: since it occupies the final slot, ja cannot follow it and sits in the Mittelfeld.

exercises.english: I would have gladly helped you.
exercises.german: Ich hätte dir ja gern geholfen.
exercises.why: Modal-like gern is an adverb, so ja precedes it in the Mittelfeld and the verb stays finite.

exercises.english: Could you just look at the timetable once?
exercises.german: Schau doch mal bitte in den Fahrplan.
exercises.why: Two particles after the imperative; separable prefix in attaches to the verb, not to the particle.

exercises.english: We would have arrived earlier, wouldn't we?
exercises.german: Wir wären wohl früher angekommen.
exercises.why: Konjunktiv II with an arrival verb; the particle cannot be moved behind the participle at the end.

exercises.english: You have already eaten, right?
exercises.german: Du hast ja schon gegessen.
exercises.why: Perfekt with sein-less gehessen: the particle keeps its place between auxiliary and adverb.

exercises.english: Since you actually know it, tell me.
exercises.german: Da du es eigentlich weißt, sag es mir.
exercises.why: A da-clause, then a main clause whose particle takes position I and is followed by a comma.
